description: Ground Truth talks from BSides Las Vegas 2025.

talks.title: Human Attack Surfaces in Agentic Web: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the AI Apocalypse
talks.teaser: Examines how AI agents could open new attack surfaces that target people, through digital twins and cognitive manipulation.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by asking whether the current AI wave is a passing fad, and argues it is not, comparing the time savings of online life with what autonomous agents could deliver. The speaker defines an agent as a system with sensors, goals, a way to update internal state, and actuators, and suggests that personal agents negotiating on people's behalf could become a new layer between users and the internet.

The middle covers attacks. Adversarial examples on vision models lead into natural-language interfaces, where phrasing and emojis can change how a model responds, and where companies may face liability for what chatbots commit to. The talk then covers agents that target humans, such as voice phishing driven by digital twins of colleagues, and sleeper-style triggers hidden in models. It introduces cognitive security as disruption of how an agent takes in information, processes it, or acts on it, including illusions and nudges.

The closing part covers audience questions on accountability, emotional attachment to AI therapists as a data risk, and the speaker's view that current models lack any sense of deception or values, so access should be limited to what one can afford to lose. Practitioners should treat agent access as a risk decision and plan for patient, personalized social engineering aimed at staff.

talks.title: A Hacker's Guide to People-Patching in 90 Days
talks.teaser: Explains how cognitive biases and phishing simulation data shape employee click behavior, and how to reduce it.
talks.summary:
The talk reframes the familiar idea that humans are the weakest link, arguing that human behavior follows predictable biology and can be strengthened instead of blamed. The speaker draws on a dataset from more than 1,300 organizations that combines training results, phishing simulation outcomes, real reporting data and survey answers. One finding is that the likelihood of a click climbs with time since training, which suggests short, regular interventions beat a single annual session.

Much of the middle focuses on why people click. In a survey of people who had clicked simulated lures, mimicry, where messages looked legitimate or matched something expected, was the most common explanation, while fear was rare. The talk covers optimism bias, overconfidence after brief training, and higher click rates among those who fully trust security tools. It also argues that long post-click education pages fail because people rarely stay long enough to read them, and that system one thinking and cognitive load explain many errors.

The closing section turns to practical design using a neuroscience-based model covering status, certainty, autonomy, relatedness and fairness. Suggested tactics include visible progress scores, winnable and fair simulations, rewards for reporting even after a click, and positive recognition in place of shame boards. Executives should be shown post-click report rates and reporter accuracy, not click rates alone. The takeaway is that people-focused programs work best as continuous, motivational loops.

talks.title: Advancing Network Threat Detection Thru Standardized Feature Extraction & Dynamic Ensemble Learning
talks.teaser: Presents an ensemble machine learning approach to network intrusion detection that aims to hold up beyond lab datasets.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a common problem with machine learning for intrusion detection: many earlier studies trained a single classifier on small, narrow datasets that looked strong in the lab but generalized poorly to real traffic, with efficacy often falling below 40 percent once models met unseen traffic. The research asks whether detection accuracy can improve by working directly from packet-level data.

The approach has three parts. First, a standardized feature extraction framework built on packet metadata and flow-level statistics, avoiding reliance on IP addresses and port numbers that do not scale to new traffic. Second, a set of classifiers that includes random forest, isolation forest, GMM, QDA, boosting methods and neural networks. Third, a custom ensemble that weights each model's output by confidence, giving more influence to less certain predictions. Training combined public labeled captures with benign traffic gathered from home and academic networks. The ensemble reached roughly 98 percent accuracy and the most balanced precision and recall among the models tested.

The speaker was clear about limits: the classifiers were static, testing used captured traffic rather than live capture, and some GMM and neural models underperformed. Future work includes tuning hyperparameters, exploring CNN and RNN approaches, and testing on live traffic, with a small Raspberry Pi prototype already being tried on open Wi-Fi. The framework is released under a GPL license. The main takeaway is that feature choice can matter as much as model choice, and that ensembles can offset individual model weaknesses.

talks.title: RAG Against the Machine: Using Retrieval-Augmented Generation & MCP to Fortify Cybersecurity Defense
talks.teaser: Shows how retrieval-augmented generation and MCP can feed threat intel and logs into LLMs for SOC triage and compliance mapping.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the pressures on security operations: alert volume, false positives, staffing gaps and burnout. The speaker argues AI should act as an assistant with a human still in the loop, and that internal data can stay private if retrieval runs in a self-hosted environment rather than a hosted service.

The core of the talk is retrieval-augmented generation, explained through a library analogy. An embedding model turns a question into searchable terms, a vector database holds chunked documents such as ATT&CK techniques, Sigma detections and advisories, and a language model writes the answer from the retrieved passages. Refreshing the index keeps answers current, unlike a static model. Guardrails covered include encrypting the store, filtering inputs and outputs, and logging activity to the SOC, and he noted that judging answer quality is hard.

Demos show an open-source tool that uses Model Context Protocol to connect the model to these sources, mapping a Splunk detection to a MITRE technique and linking related threat intel. A second tool classifies uploaded policies with a BERT-based model to estimate coverage against frameworks such as SOC 2. He closes by urging practitioners to start small, test with their own data and press vendors on cost and token transparency. In Q&A he suggested running open-source models locally to cut costs.

talks.title: Indexing the Chaos: Extract PII from Ransomware Leaks
talks.teaser: Explains how personal data is pulled out of ransomware-leaked dumps and organized into a searchable index.

talks.title: Autonomous Discovery of Logic-based API Vulnerabilities
talks.teaser: Shows reinforcement learning agents navigating API graphs to find broken access control and other logic flaws.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by comparing static analysis, dynamic scanners and LLM-based tooling against logic flaws such as broken access control and privilege escalation. The speakers argue these bugs depend on application state, user roles and multi-step request sequences rather than a single malicious input, so input-focused fuzzing struggles with them. They also point out that LLM agents are slow, limited by context size and reliant on scripts for bulk testing.

The middle of the talk frames the search as a reinforcement learning problem. The application is modeled as a tree of endpoints, request and response pairs, authentication contexts and parameters, which a graph neural network encodes. The agent moves through this graph and can copy values such as identifiers or tokens from one request into another. To train and benchmark it, the team generates many small applications from YAML-defined components, each with vulnerable or patched variants. In a simple demo, the agent reuses another user's token to act on that user's notes, and it reached this path without being given strategies or example traces.

The closing part covers questions about benchmark ground truth, comparisons with Burp-style fuzzing and the need to rebuild the graph for each new application, which can be seeded from a crawl. The speakers said the lab generator will be open-sourced and that the work is early. The practical takeaway is that a dedicated method per vulnerability class may suit logic flaws better than one general-purpose model.

talks.title: Predicting the Lifespans of Internet Services: Falling down the ML Rabbit Hole, and What We Learned From The Thud
talks.teaser: Walks through failed machine learning attempts to predict how long internet services stay online, and the classifier that worked.
talks.summary:
Ariana Mirian, a researcher at an internet scanning company, describes why hourly scan data was hard to trust. Many hosts are ephemeral, appearing and vanishing between checks, so the team set out to predict how long each service would stay up, which could guide how often it gets rescanned.

Regression failed first. Port, protocol and autonomous system are categorical, and one-hot encoding left very sparse matrices given roughly 40 ports, 300 protocols and 19,000 autonomous systems. Grouping autonomous systems helped little, R-squared stayed around 0.3 at best, and feature rankings changed from model to model. Seeing that most hosts lived long with a small short-lived tail, the team switched to classifying hosts as under or over 12 hours. Several classifiers agreed on feature importance, reaching about 87 percent accuracy and a 0.94 ROC AUC, with autonomous system ranked highest. Software attributes such as vendor and version ranked low next to network-level features.

The takeaways were as much about process as models. Experts from both networking and machine learning were needed, since dropping autonomous system was rejected on domain grounds. Reframing the question was worth more than tuning, and an actionable answer beat a publishable one. In the Q&A, the speaker explained that scanner speed was tuned against known-live hosts and that a one-hour gap was counted as a false negative, while retries were skipped in the experiment due to scan budget.

talks.title: Automating Phishing Infrastructure Development Using AI Agents
talks.teaser: Shows how AI agents can automate a phishing chain, from target profiling to domain purchase and site setup.
talks.summary:
Fred Heiding and Simon Lermen present research on using AI agents to automate phishing from start to finish, not just to draft emails. They recap an earlier study in which AI-written emails performed about as well as those from human experts, then describe newer work where an agent gathers public information about a target, writes a personalized message, and adjusts its persuasion style over repeated attempts. The work extends to voice phishing, and a live demo showed an AI caller asking a volunteer for an email address.

The middle of the talk covers the supporting infrastructure. The speakers describe an agent that searches domain registrar APIs, compares prices, favours cheap domain endings, buys a domain, configures DNS and certificates, and deploys a cloned or generated website. They note that some models could be steered past safety filters with simple prompts, and that cloning a site from screenshots is easy. Cost figures were given for a one-minute AI voice call, around ten cents, to show how cheap sophisticated attacks are becoming.

For defenders, the speakers suggest priming AI classifiers to look for suspicion, which they say raised true detections without increasing false positives. They also propose personalized spam filters, stricter know-your-customer checks for domain registration, and better protection for older adults, who are heavily targeted by scams. The takeaway is that the cost of convincing social engineering is falling, so defensive budgets and research need to keep pace.

talks.title: Securing AI Infrastructure: Lessons from National Cybersecurity Strategies and Attacks Against Other Critical Sectors
talks.teaser: Connects past breaches in other critical sectors to AI labs and compares national cyber strategies from several countries.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that AI labs are attractive espionage targets and that the AI sector is not yet treated as a dedicated critical infrastructure sector in the US. The speakers draw on a study of more than 200 cyber attacks, insider threats and espionage cases across industries such as semiconductors and biotech, tracking what happened to victims and their wider sectors afterward.

The findings they described include lasting revenue drops for breached firms, damage that spreads across an entire sector, a shift from trade secrets toward patents, and a sharp decline in Asian research staff after incidents. That last point suggests a need for response plans that avoid panic-driven responses. They also reviewed national cyber strategies from countries including the US, Australia, Singapore and the UK. AI is often covered in these documents, but securing it receives less attention than AI safety, and metrics, incentives and clear accountability are weak.

Recommendations included defining concrete security requirements for AI as critical infrastructure, separating incident reporting from law enforcement as Australia has done, and using UK-style programs in which industry staff hold pre-approved clearances while keeping their jobs. They also called for wider security clearance coverage and more non-technical cyber expertise in law and policy. The session closed with audience questions on using supply chain leverage and on incentive structures.

talks.title: How Conflict Leads to Innovation
talks.teaser: Walks through the TRIZ problem-solving method and shows how it applies to security problems like supply chains and ICS.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces TRIZ, a structured method for resolving contradictions instead of settling for compromise. The speaker traces its origin to a Soviet patent researcher who developed the framework from patterns found across thousands of inventions, and explains that the method starts by stating the conflict clearly, then working through a matrix of recurring principles to find solutions that remove the trade-off.

Physical examples carried the explanation, including a wrench with a ratcheting head, a keyboard without key legends, a key switch that ejects its key when turned off, and an air conditioner that moves its noisy compressor outside. Business cases followed, such as a company that reframed security as something that supports openness, and a test-data approach that split sensitive records from low-risk ones.

For security, the speaker applied the same thinking to data privacy, dark web markets where anonymity competes with trust, software supply chains where fast deployment conflicts with checking transitive dependencies, industrial control segmentation focused on availability, and insider monitoring versus employee autonomy. The method suits recurring conflicts rather than one-off incidents, and results still need domain experts to validate them. The takeaway is to name the contradiction precisely before looking for a fix.

talks.title: Fragmentation of CTI: The Deck is Stacked Against the Defenders
talks.teaser: Applies the STPA-Sec systems safety method to find hazards and unsafe control actions in AI coding and intelligence-analysis systems.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces STPA-Sec, a systems-theoretic hazard analysis method extended to cover security, and argues that traditional failure analysis misses how AI systems can go wrong without any component breaking. The presenters frame safety as a control problem and walk through the core vocabulary: losses, system-level hazards, and the four categories of unsafe control action.

Two case studies follow. The first models an AI coding assistant, with a developer, an agent plugin, an IDE, logging, and a training pipeline acting as controllers. The hazards they list include vulnerable code accepted without review, proprietary code leaking through feedback logs, and updates that introduce regressions. The second covers an analyst using an LLM to digest open-source intelligence, where confident fabrication becomes the central hazard. A later point adds a repository README carrying adversarial instructions that an AI tool could follow after cloning, which widens the modeled attack surface.

The method then moves from hazards to mitigation: deriving formal safety and security constraints, building behavior models, generating test cases, and wargaming adversary actions with red and blue teams. The closing takeaways stress bringing risk, compliance and governance into design early and iterating across the lifecycle. In the Q&A, the presenters share examples of a radar gain control that suppressed real targets and adversarial patches that could disable a camera-based detection system, arguing that robustness testing must feed back into design.

talks.title: Increasing Complexity and Frequency of Cyber Events: Trends, Costs, and Risk Mitigation Strategies
talks.teaser: Surveys cyber insurance claims data to trace ransomware, business interruption, and privacy litigation trends and their costs.
talks.summary:
The session comes from a cyber insurance broker's perspective, drawing on annual insurance applications, client claims, reinsurance portfolio data and public sources. The speaker reviews where cyber losses are heading: event frequency is up, the share of extortion and ransomware events has slipped, and the share of companies paying ransoms dropped to about 18 percent. Wire fraud tied to business email compromise is climbing sharply.

Privacy regulation gets the most attention. The speaker walks through state-level laws such as CIPA and BIPA, website tracking and SDK-related litigation, and large fines and settlements. Business interruption is another major cost driver, illustrated by the CrowdStrike and healthcare outages, with claim adjustment often running a year or more because of disputes over proof of loss and forensic accounting. Third-party and supplier dependencies are flagged as a growing source of disruption.

For mitigation, the speaker points to controls correlated with lower breach likelihood, including phishing-resistant MFA, endpoint detection coverage, and privileged access management. Faster claims handling comes from pre-approved forensic accountants and tabletop exercises. Data minimization, classifying and deleting unneeded data, and privacy-enhancing techniques such as differential privacy and federated learning are presented as ways to reduce exposure.

talks.title: A Winning Competition
talks.teaser: Explains how collegiate cyber competitions like WRCCDC and CIRCUS get designed, and how to grow them into events people return to.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a longtime competition volunteer, explains how collegiate cyber competitions are designed and how they can grow from events people merely take part in into ones they want to return to. The talk sorts competitions into capture-the-flag events, attack-and-defend contests such as CCDC, and red-team or forensics formats. It then focuses on two examples: the Western regional CCDC, and CIRCUS, a newer incident response contest for undergraduates that started at a community college.

Much of the talk covers logistics and balance. Organizers must decide where infrastructure lives between events, how competitors log in and receive credentials, what always-on hosting costs, and whether multi-day events pay off. If a contest is too hard, newcomers drop out, so tiered entry points such as invitational events help feed students into the main competition. An emergency shutdown of hosted servers during the speaker's first event showed why backups and contingency plans matter. According to the speaker, discouragement came less from difficulty than from small frustrations and a lack of feedback.

The closing advice is aimed at organizers, coaches and academic programs: share past resources and training material, keep notes so later teams can build on earlier work, keep competitors and organizers separate, and ask what will bring students and volunteers back next year. The speaker linked these changes to the regional team's rise from never placing first at nationals to recent wins.

talks.title: Mental Models to Anticipate the Next Stages of the AI and Cybersecurity Revolution
talks.teaser: Presents mental models for forecasting how AI reshapes security decisions, from agentic automation to organizational controls.
talks.summary:
Sounil Yu frames the talk as a search for ground truth in security, arguing that mental models give practitioners a shared vocabulary for hard questions about AI. He combines several of them: a risk-focused version of the serenity prayer, the Cynefin framework for deciding when to run experiments versus automate, and the DIKW pyramid, which he uses to map familiar data problems onto knowledge problems raised by large language models.

He then applies the models to automation. He recasts the OODA loop as sensing, sense making, decision making and acting, and shows that each stage handed to a machine needs its own controls, with agentic AI requiring controls over decisions. He argues that agent experiments are most valuable for discovering better business processes, and that job losses often follow process redesign rather than AI alone. He compares language models to fast, intuitive thinking and suggests that structured frameworks can supply the slower checking layer, drawing on organizational typologies and a balance of generative, bureaucratic and pathological functions.

He closes by warning that every model is incomplete, so a useful test is whether a claim fits the model at hand. When it does not, either the claim or the model may be wrong. In audience questions he discussed whether a model must want honesty rather than just know it, and where a reasoning layer sits relative to the model. The practical takeaway is to combine a few models to evaluate vendor and AI claims.
